--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.match()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Find the matches of a Cypher MATCH pattern, as a table. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.match()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Find the matches of a Cypher MATCH pattern, as a table. title: >- [Graph.match()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Find the matches of a Cypher MATCH pattern, as a table. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the matches of a Cypher `MATCH` pattern, as a table. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L24858-L25270){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.match( query, params=None, limit=None, use_labels=False, distinct_nodes=False, label_key="name", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Match a pattern](/assets/graphs/match.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed six-node grid A to F, each node tagged with its integer id 1 to 6, where B and C point at each other and so do D and E. The query MATCH (a)-->(b)-->(a) finds the 2-cycles, and the result is a table with columns a and b holding node ids, one row per match: 2 3, 3 2, 4 5, and 5 4. Each cycle matches twice, once from each end. The first row and its match, B and C with both edges, are in the accent color." width="100%"} Each match of the pattern is one row of a Polars DataFrame, and each named variable is a column holding the ID of the node or edge it matched (or the list of edge IDs, for a variable-length relationship, and the nodes and edges of a path variable). The ID columns join directly onto `get_node_df()` and `get_edge_df()`, and Polars takes over from there. To act on the matches instead, use `select_match()`, and to count them, `count_matches()`. The query is one or more `MATCH` clauses, each with an optional `WHERE`, and then an optional `RETURN`. `WITH` can split it into parts, each of which runs on the rows of the one before: - **Patterns:** nodes such as `(p:Person {born: 1964})` and relationships such as `-[r:ACTED_IN]->`, `<-[:KNOWS]-` or `--`. Several patterns can be listed with commas, and they share variables. - **Variable-length relationships:** `-[:KNOWS*1..3]->` follows one to three `KNOWS` relationships in a row. `*2` means exactly two, `*` one or more, `*..3` up to three, and `*0..` allows zero, which makes both ends the same node. - **Path variables:** `p = (a)-[:KNOWS*]->(b)-->(c)` names the whole path a pattern matched, from its first node to its last. - **Shortest paths:** `shortestPath((a)-[*]-(b))` matches one shortest path between each pair of nodes `a` and `b`, and `allShortestPaths((a)-[*]-(b))` every path of that least length. The pattern is one variable-length relationship, which may have types, properties and an upper bound (and a lower bound of 0 or 1), and it can be named, as in `p = shortestPath(...)`. - **Several clauses:** `MATCH (p:Person) MATCH (p)-->(m)` extends each match of the first clause with the matches of the second, which share its variables. `OPTIONAL MATCH` does the same, but keeps a row that it can't extend, with its new variables `null`. - **`WHERE`:** comparisons (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`), `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `NOT`, `IS NULL`, `IN [...]`, `STARTS WITH`, `ENDS WITH`, `CONTAINS`, `=~` (a regular expression that must match the whole string), label tests (`n:Person`), and the functions `id()`, `type()`, `labels()`, `size()`, `toLower()`, `toUpper()`, `exists()`, and, for path variables, `length()` (the number of relationships), `nodes()` and `relationships()`. Each `WHERE` belongs to its clause, and sees that clause's variables and those of the clauses before it. - **`RETURN`:** chooses the columns, in order. Each is an expression, such as a variable (`RETURN p, m`), a property (`p.name`), a function call (`length(path)`, `toLower(p.name)`, `nodes(path)`), a comparison or a list (`[p.name, p.born]`), and `AS` names it (`RETURN length(path) AS hops`). Without `AS`, a variable's column is named after it, a property's after the variable and key (`"p.name"`), and anything else after the expression as written. `RETURN *` returns every named variable, and can be followed by more columns (`RETURN *, p.name AS name`). `RETURN DISTINCT` drops repeated rows. - **Aggregation:** `count(*)` counts rows, and `count(x)`, `collect(x)`, `sum(x)`, `avg(x)`, `min(x)` and `max(x)` fold the values of `x`, as in `RETURN m.title, count(*) AS n`. The columns without an aggregating function are the grouping keys: the rows that agree on all of them make one row of the table, and with no keys, all the rows make one (even when nothing matches). `DISTINCT` inside the call (`count(DISTINCT p)`) folds each different value once. An aggregation can sit inside an expression (`size(collect(m))`), which may also use the grouping keys (`[m.title, count(*)]`). - **`ORDER BY`, `SKIP` and `LIMIT`:** these follow `RETURN`, in that order. `ORDER BY p.born DESC, p.name` sorts the rows by one or more expressions (`ASC`, the default, or `DESC`), which may use the names of the `RETURN` columns; after `RETURN DISTINCT` or an aggregation, it can only use the returned columns (and expressions of them). `SKIP 2` drops the first two rows and `LIMIT 5` keeps at most five; each takes a non-negative integer or a parameter (`LIMIT $n`). - **`WITH`:** ends a part of the query, and passes its rows on to the next part, which starts with a `MATCH` (or another `WITH`) and ends with the next `WITH` or the end of the query. `WITH` lists columns as `RETURN` does, and can be `DISTINCT`, aggregate, and have `ORDER BY`, `SKIP` and `LIMIT`; then an optional `WHERE` filters its rows. So `MATCH (p)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m) WITH m, count(*) AS n WHERE n > 1` keeps the movies with more than one actor, and `WITH p ORDER BY p.born LIMIT 3` the three oldest people, for the rest of the query to go on from. Each expression that isn't a variable needs a name (`WITH p.name AS name`), and the next part sees only the columns `WITH` lists (`WITH *` lists every named variable). The query reads EdgeCase graphs the way `from_cypher()` writes them: - a node's labels are its `type` attribute (a string, or a list for several labels); - a relationship's type is its `rel` attribute; - `n.name` reads the node's label when the node has no `name` attribute (see `label_key=`); - `r.weight` reads the edge weight; - any other property is the attribute, and a missing attribute is `null`. Matching follows Cypher's rules: - **Edges:** within one clause of a match each edge is used at most once, but a node may appear more than once. So `(a)-->(b)-->(a)` finds 2-cycles. `distinct_nodes=True` makes the nodes distinct as well, as in `subgraph_isomorphisms()`. Separate clauses may reuse edges and nodes, and a relationship variable that appears in a later clause is the same edge there. - **Variable-length relationships:** each path is its own match, so two routes between the same nodes give two rows. The column lists the path's edges in the order the pattern runs, and the relationship's types and properties apply to every edge on it. In `WHERE`, `size(r)` is the number of edges, but a path has no properties of its own. Without an upper bound, the number of paths can grow very fast on dense graphs. - **Path variables:** a path lists its nodes and its edges in the order the pattern runs, and a node appears again each time the path comes back to it. In `WHERE`, a path has no properties; use `length(p)`, `nodes(p)` and `relationships(p)`. - **Shortest paths:** the edges of a shortest path follow the same rules as a variable-length relationship: each is used once, it avoids the other edges of its clause, and with `distinct_nodes=True` it visits no node twice. A `WHERE` condition on the path (or its relationship variable) is part of what "shortest" means, so `WHERE length(p) > 2` finds the shortest paths longer than 2, rather than dropping the shortest paths if they're too short. When `a` and `b` are the same node, the shortest path is the shortest cycle through it (of length 0 with `*0..`), where Neo4j raises an error. A breadth-first search guides the search for shortest paths, so they don't need an upper bound the way a variable-length relationship does, and `shortestPath()` keeps the first one it finds. - **Parallel edges and self-loops:** each parallel edge gives its own match, and a self-loop matches `(a)-->(a)`. - **Undirected graphs:** every relationship matches in either direction, so `-->`, `<--` and `--` mean the same, and an edge between `a` and `b` matches `(x)--(y)` twice: once with `x = a` and once with `x = b`. - **`null`:** a comparison with a missing property or a `null` variable is `null`, and `WHERE` keeps a row only when its condition is `true`. A later pattern that uses a variable that `OPTIONAL MATCH` left `null` matches nothing. Values of different types compare as unequal, and can't be ordered, so `'3' < 4` is `null`. A pattern property such as `{age: null}` never matches. - **`ORDER BY`:** unlike a comparison, `ORDER BY` can sort any values. Values of one type sort in their own order (nodes and relationships by ID), and values of different types in Cypher's order: maps, nodes, relationships, lists, paths, strings, booleans, then numbers, with `null` last (and so first with `DESC`). - **Aggregation:** every aggregating function skips `null`s, so `count(x)` counts the rows where `x` isn't `null`. `collect()` lists the values in row order, `sum()` adds numbers (giving 0 when there are none, and an integer for integers), `avg()` gives a float, and `min()` and `max()` take the smallest and largest values in `ORDER BY`'s order, so they work on any values. `avg()`, `min()` and `max()` of no values are `null`. Grouping keys and `DISTINCT` compare values as `RETURN DISTINCT` does, where `1` and `1.0` are the same value and so are any two NaNs. - **`WITH`:** the next part runs once for each row of `WITH`, with its columns bound, so `WITH m MATCH (m)<--(q)` extends each movie with its neighbors, and a row that the next part can't extend is dropped (but kept by `OPTIONAL MATCH`). A column that holds a node or relationship, such as `m`, `r` or `max(m)`, can be used in the patterns of the next part, and one that holds another value only in expressions. The `WHERE` of `WITH` comes after its `ORDER BY`, `SKIP` and `LIMIT`, and sees only its columns. A variable that `WITH` doesn't list is gone from the next part, which can use its name for a new variable. Without `ORDER BY`, rows are sorted by the IDs of the named variables, in the order they first appear in the query (with `null` last), so the same query on the same graph always gives the same table. `ORDER BY` keeps that order for rows that tie on every key, `RETURN DISTINCT` keeps each row at the place of its first match, and an aggregation puts each group at the place of its first row. After `WITH`, the rows follow the order of the rows of `WITH`, and for each of those, the IDs of the variables that the part adds. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [query]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The Cypher text, such as `"MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m) WHERE m.released > 2000"`. Keywords ignore case. Anything outside the supported subset raises a `ValueError` that gives the line and column. [params]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[dict]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Values for the `$name` parameters in the query, as a dict such as `{"year": 1999}`. Parameters keep values (especially strings) out of the query text, so they need no quoting. `$0` reads the key `0` or `"0"`. [limit]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The most matches to find, or `None` (the default) for all of them. The search stops once it has found this many, so the table holds the first rows found, sorted, rather than the rows with the smallest IDs. With `RETURN DISTINCT`, it counts distinct rows, and with aggregation, the groups are made from the matches it found. It applies before `ORDER BY`, `SKIP` and `LIMIT` in the query, which sort and slice the rows it found; it's a cap on the work, while the query's own `LIMIT` gives the top rows of the full result. After `WITH`, it applies to the last part only, so the parts before it see every match. [use_labels]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, nodes show as their labels instead of IDs, in node columns and inside values such as `nodes(p)` or `[a, b]`. Edges have no labels, so relationships always show as edge IDs. `ORDER BY` still sorts nodes by ID. [distinct_nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, the nodes of each clause of a match must all be different, anonymous ones and the inner nodes of variable-length paths included, as in a subgraph isomorphism. A variable that appears twice is still one node. The default follows Cypher, where only the edges must differ. [label_key]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["name"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The property that reads the node label when a node has no attribute of that name. The default, `"name"`, matches `from_cypher()`, which turns `name` into the label. Use `None` to read only attributes. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pl.DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One row per match (or per group, with aggregation). Without `RETURN`, there is one column per named variable, holding node or edge IDs (`Int64`), node labels with `use_labels=True`, or lists of edge IDs (`List(Int64)`) for variable-length relationships. A path variable's column is a struct with the fields `nodes` (its node IDs, or labels with `use_labels=True`) and `relationships` (its edge IDs), both lists; `.struct.field()` or `unnest()` takes them apart. With `RETURN`, the columns are the ones it lists: variables as above, `id()`, `size()` and `length()` as `Int64`, `type()`, `toLower()` and `toUpper()` as `String`, `labels()` as `List(String)`, conditions as `Boolean`, `nodes()` and `relationships()` as lists of IDs (or labels, for nodes with `use_labels=True`), `count()` as `Int64`, `avg()` as `Float64`, `collect()` as a list, and properties and other expressions with the type of their values. Variables that `OPTIONAL MATCH` found nothing for are `null`. A query without matches gives an empty table with the same columns. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the query has a syntax error, uses something outside the supported subset, refers to an unknown variable or function, needs a parameter that `params=` doesn't give, or meets a value of the wrong type (such as `WHERE n.name` on a string, `toLower(n.born)` on a number, or `sum()` of strings). Also if there is no `RETURN` and the query names no variables (so there would be no columns), if `RETURN` gives two columns the same name, if an aggregating function is outside `RETURN` and `ORDER BY` or inside another, if a column beside an aggregation uses a variable that isn't a grouping key, if `WITH` lists an expression without a name, if a part uses a variable that the `WITH` before it doesn't list, if a pattern uses a column of `WITH` that holds a value (and not a node or relationship), if the query ends with `WITH`, if `SKIP` or `LIMIT` isn't a non-negative integer, or if `limit=` isn't one. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `query=` isn't a string, `params=` isn't a dict, or `label_key=` isn't a string or `None`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A small movie graph, built from Cypher with `from_cypher()`: ::: {#6145e4be .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.from_cypher(""" CREATE (keanu:Person {name: 'Keanu Reeves', born: 1964}), (carrie:Person {name: 'Carrie-Anne Moss', born: 1967}), (lana:Person {name: 'Lana Wachowski', born: 1965}), (matrix:Movie {title: 'The Matrix', released: 1999}), (wick:Movie {title: 'John Wick', released: 2014}), (keanu)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Neo']}]->(matrix), (carrie)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Trinity']}]->(matrix), (keanu)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['John Wick']}]->(wick), (lana)-[:DIRECTED]->(matrix) """) graph.match("MATCH (p:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Each row is one acting credit, and the columns hold node and edge IDs. `use_labels=True` shows the node labels instead (the movies have no `name`, so `from_cypher()` labeled them with their variables): ::: {#debb9d19 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match("MATCH (p:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)", use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

p.namep.born

Here, two people who acted in the same movie (`id(a) < id(b)` keeps one row per pair): ::: {#02eced44 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH (a:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m)<-[:ACTED_IN]-(b:Person) WHERE id(a) < id(b) " "RETURN a.name, b.name, m.title" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 3)
a.nameb.namem.title
strstrstr
"Keanu Reeves""Carrie-Anne Moss""The Matrix"
``` ::: ::: A variable-length relationship follows several hops. The people two steps from Lana Wachowski are the ones who worked on one of her movies: ::: {#2607f5bc .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH (:Person {name: 'Lana Wachowski'})-[r*2]-(b:Person) RETURN b.name, r" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 2)
b.namer

"Keanu Reeves"[4, 1]
"Carrie-Anne Moss"[4, 2]
``` ::: ::: A path variable holds the whole path, as a struct of its nodes and its edges. Here, the shortest path from Carrie-Anne Moss to Lana Wachowski, with `use_labels=True` to show the nodes as labels: ::: {#fd55ab65 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH p = shortestPath(" "(:Person {name: 'Carrie-Anne Moss'})-[*]-(:Person {name: 'Lana Wachowski'}))", use_labels=True, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 1)
p
struct[2]
{["Carrie-Anne Moss", "matrix", "Lana Wachowski"],[2, 4]}
``` ::: ::: `RETURN` can compute columns and name them with `AS`, and `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` give the top rows. Here, the two youngest people: ::: {#8d345db9 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.name AS name, p.born AS born " "ORDER BY born DESC LIMIT 2" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 2)
nameborn
stri64
"Carrie-Anne Moss"1967
"Lana Wachowski"1965
``` ::: ::: Path functions work in `RETURN` too. The number of hops from Carrie-Anne Moss to everyone else, closest first: ::: {#f10faaaf .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH p = shortestPath((:Person {name: 'Carrie-Anne Moss'})-[*]-(b)) " "RETURN b.name AS name, length(p) AS hops, nodes(p) AS route " "ORDER BY hops, name", use_labels=True, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

namehopsroute

"Keanu Reeves"2["Carrie-Anne Moss", "matrix", "Keanu Reeves"]
"Lana Wachowski"2["Carrie-Anne Moss", "matrix", "Lana Wachowski"]
"wick"3["Carrie-Anne Moss", "matrix", … "wick"]
``` ::: ::: `OPTIONAL MATCH` keeps the rows it can't extend, with `null` for what it didn't find: ::: {#e0d0c146 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH (p:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:DIRECTED]->(m) RETURN p.name, m.title" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 2)
p.namem.title

"Carrie-Anne Moss"null

Here, each person's movies, most first: ::: {#933824e3 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) " "RETURN p.name AS name, count(*) AS movies, collect(m.title) AS titles " "ORDER BY movies DESC, name" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 3)
namemoviestitles

"Carrie-Anne Moss"1["The Matrix"]
``` ::: ::: Without other columns, the whole match is one group: ::: {#b13d0fe1 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.match( "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN count(*) AS people, min(p.born) AS oldest, avg(p.born)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
